title: Evolutionary history and ecology context shape mixed paternity across birds
text:
A global comparative phylogenetic meta-analysis of mixed-paternity prevalence across avian species.
375 species · 619 population estimates · 46,249 broods



This website presents the complete reproducible workflow for the flobal comparative meta-analysis of mixed-paternity prevalence across birds.






Core idea



Birds are central model systems for studying sexual selection and reproductive conflict, yet mixed-paternity prevalence is often comparatively low across species. This study aims to understand which ecological, social, and methodological factors explain variation in mixed paternity across birds.

title: 3  Data preparation
text:
3.3 Prepare data

3.3.1 Population identifier
Population identity was defined using study identity and rounded geographic coordinates, with latitude and longitude rounded to two decimal places prior to constructing the population identifier.


Code
mixed_pat <- mixed_pat_raw %>%
  mutate(
    Lat_round = round(Lat, 2),
    Long_round = round(Long, 2),
    population_id = paste(Study_ID, Lat_round, Long_round, sep = "_"),
    population_id = as.factor(population_id)
  )




3.3.2 Study and species formatting
The following step formats the main grouping variables used in the models and calculates the total number of broods by combining mixed- and non-mixed-brood counts.


Code
mixed_pat <- mixed_pat %>%
  mutate(
    Study_ID = as.factor(Study_ID),
    species_phylo_brms = as.factor(Clements_name),
    species_nonphylo = as.factor(Clements_name),

    n_mixed_broods = as.numeric(n_mixed_broods),
    n_non_mixed_broods = as.numeric(n_non_mixed_broods),
    n_total_broods = n_mixed_broods + n_non_mixed_broods
  )




3.3.3 Phylogeny preparation
Species names were harmonised between the mixed-paternity dataset and the phylogenetic tree prior to pruning the tree and generating the phylogenetic covariance matrix used in the Bayesian models.


Code
species_data <- mixed_pat %>%
  filter(!is.na(species_phylo_brms)) %>%
  pull(species_phylo_brms) %>%
  as.character() %>%
  unique()

species_tree <- tree$tip.label

species_for_tree <- intersect(species_data, species_tree)

tree_analysis <- ape::keep.tip(tree, species_for_tree)

phylo_mat <- ape::vcv.phylo(tree_analysis, corr = TRUE)

phylo_mat <- phylo_mat[
  sort(rownames(phylo_mat)),
  sort(colnames(phylo_mat))
]

mixed_pat <- mixed_pat %>%
  filter(species_phylo_brms %in% rownames(phylo_mat)) %>%
  mutate(
    species_phylo_brms = droplevels(species_phylo_brms),
    species_nonphylo = droplevels(species_nonphylo)
  )




3.3.4 Phylogeny - summary

  Item = c(
    "Species matched to phylogeny",

  ),

    length(species_for_tree),

title: 4  Overall model
text: 4.4 Modelling framework Because brood-level paternity data are expected to exhibit substantial extra-binomial heterogeneity across references, populations, and species, we modelled mixed-paternity prevalence using beta-binomial generalised linear mixed-effects models with a logit link: \[y_i \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n_i, \mu_i, \phi)\] where \(y_i\) is the number of broods with mixed paternity, \(n_i\) is the total number of broods genotyped, \(\mu_i\) is the expected mixed-paternity prevalence, and the precision parameter \(\phi\) describes extra-binomial variation among study units. The linear predictor was modelled as: \[\mathrm{logit}(\mu_i) = \alpha + \mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta} + u_{\mathrm{reference}[i]} + u_{\mathrm{species}[i]} + u_{\mathrm{phylo}[i]}\] where \(\alpha\) is the intercept, \(\mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}\) represents fixed biological and methodological moderators, and \(u_{\mathrm{reference}}\) , \(u_{\mathrm{species}}\) , and \(u_{\mathrm{phylo}}\) represent study-identity-level, non-phylogenetic species-level, and phylogenetically structured random effects, respectively. Study identity ( Study_ID ) is an analytical grouping variable, not a bibliographic-publication count; one study identity can incorporate evidence reported across more than one source.

title: 4  Overall model
text:
4.5 Overall mixed-paternity prevalence

4.5.1 Model
The intercept-only model estimated the average mixed-paternity prevalence across studies and species while accounting for study-level, non-phylogenetic species-level, and phylogenetically structured species-level variation.


Code
model_overall_study <- brm(
  n_mixed_broods | trials(n_total_broods) ~
    1 +
    (1 | Study_ID) +
    (1 | species_nonphylo) +
    (1 | gr(species_phylo_brms, cov = phylo_mat)),
  family = beta_binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = data_overall_study,
  data2 = list(phylo_mat = phylo_mat),
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  iter = 10000,
  warmup = 5000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 15),
  seed = 123
)

4.5.5 Phylogenetic signal
We quantified the phylogenetic signal in between-species variation as the proportion of species-level variance attributable to the phylogenetically structured random effect:
\[
\nu =
\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{phylo}}}
{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{phylo}} + \sigma^2_{\mathrm{nonphylo}}}
\]
where \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{phylo}}\) is the variance of the phylogenetically structured species-level random effect and \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nonphylo}}\) is the variance of the non-phylogenetic species-level random effect.

text: 5 Methodological moderators Code Show All Code Hide All Code View Source This section presents methodological moderators that may influence estimates of mixed-paternity prevalence across studies. We focus on marker type, nest-box use, nest type, and study duration, because these variables can affect both the detection and reporting of mixed paternity. All models use the same multilevel phylogenetic beta-binomial structure as the overall model. Model-based prevalence is summarised as the posterior mean on the probability scale, with 95% equal-tailed credible intervals. The inverse-logit transformation is applied to each posterior draw before averaging; all random effects are set to zero. 5.1 Packages The R packages required for model fitting. title: 5  Methodological moderators
text: 5.6 Study duration Study duration was included as a methodological moderator because longer studies may provide more stable estimates of mixed-paternity prevalence and may differ from short-term studies in sampling intensity and temporal coverage. It was standardised using all 607 non-missing records in the 619-record overall analytical dataset (mean = 3.649 years, SD = 3.452 years). 5.6.1 Figure Figure 5.1: Population-level predicted mixed-paternity prevalence across study duration from the refitted single-moderator model. Study duration was standardised using the overall analytical dataset; points show observed record-level prevalence and the ribbon shows the 95% credible interval. 5.6.2 Model summary 5.6.3 Model estimates Parameter Estimate Lower 95% CrI Upper 95% CrI Study duration (per 1 SD = 3.452 years) -0.088 -0.167 -0.009 Longer studies were associated with lower mixed-paternity prevalence on the log-odds scale ( \(\beta\) = -0.088, 95% CrI -0.167 to -0.009).

title: 5  Methodological moderators
text: 5.7 Nest box Nest-box use was included as a methodological moderator because studies conducted in nest-box populations may differ from studies of natural nests in monitoring accessibility, sampling completeness, and opportunities for detecting mixed paternity. This variable may also capture biological differences associated with nesting-site availability, breeding density, and local neighbourhood structure. The intercept represents the reference category - natural nests . 5.7.1 Figure Code 5.7.2 Model summary Code 5.7.3 Model estimates Parameter Estimate Lower 95% CrI Upper 95% CrI Intercept -0.789 -2.460 0.968 nest_box_modelyes 0.285 -0.062 0.632 The nest-box model estimated a positive but uncertain association between nest-box use and mixed-paternity prevalence. Compared with natural nests, nest-box studies had a higher estimated log-odds of mixed paternity, although the 95% credible interval overlapped zero.

title: 7  Biological moderators
text: 7 Biological moderators Code Show All Code Hide All Code View Source This section presents single-moderator models for ecological, life-history, and geographic predictors of brood-level mixed paternity. These models evaluate whether mixed-paternity prevalence varies with nest type, migration status, coloniality, clutch size, body mass, and absolute latitude, while retaining the same multilevel phylogenetic beta-binomial structure used in the overall model. Model-based prevalence is summarised as the posterior mean on the probability scale, with 95% equal-tailed credible intervals. Code 7.4 Nest type architecture This model tested whether mixed-paternity prevalence differed among nest-type categories. Nest type was derived from BIRDBASE and simplified into four broad nest-architecture categories: cavity, ground, open, and other enclosed nests. text: 7.7 Clutch size This model tested whether mixed-paternity prevalence was associated with maximum clutch size. title: 7  Biological moderators
text: 7.8 Body mass This model tested whether mixed-paternity prevalence was associated with adult body mass. Body mass was log10-transformed and then standardised using all 619 records in the overall analytical dataset (mean = 1.727 log10[g], SD = 0.750 log10[g]). The coefficient therefore represents the change in log-odds per one standard deviation increase in log10-transformed body mass. 7.8.1 Figure Figure 7.2: Population-level predicted mixed-paternity prevalence across log10 adult body mass from the refitted single-moderator model. Figure generation reads saved fits and uses posterior means and equal-tailed intervals for prevalence predictions; it does not refit the models. The code below records the common-scaling preparation, model specifications and figure generation. These code blocks are displayed without execution during website rendering. Code: common scaling and data preparation Code: four continuous-moderator models Code: full multivariable model Code: continuous and full-model figures 8.3 Phylogeny plot Code Code Code Descriptive phylogenetic visualisation of the 375 species included in the final overall meta-analytic model. Radial-bar colour shows pooled observed mixed-paternity prevalence (total mixed-paternity broods divided by total broods sampled). Radial-bar height shows sampling support using log10(total broods + 1); the support key below the tree uses exactly the same transformation and reports the original brood counts. The outer categorical ring shows migratory status using the two analytical categories; missing values are grey. All species-level tracks are descriptive observations, not phylogenetically adjusted model predictions. The source tree contains 393 taxa, but the figure is restricted to the 375 species represented in the final overall-model dataset. The 18 excluded tips have neither mixed-brood counts nor brood denominators and therefore have no observed prevalence for the final meta-analysis. Pruning is applied only to the descriptive figure; the stored source tree and all analytical objects are unchanged. 8.4 Geographic distribution of study populations Code Validation of geographic map data check value Unique plotted coordinates 498 Minimum number of study identities 1 Maximum number of study identities 11 Minimum pooled prevalence 0 Maximum pooled prevalence 1 Geocoded records with missing or invalid brood denominator 53 Geocoded records with a zero brood denominator 0 Plotted prevalence values outside 0-1 0 Pooled mixed-brood total 15808 Pooled total-brood denominator 45114 Code Global geographic distribution of analytical study identities included in the comparative meta-analysis of avian mixed paternity. Radial-bar colour shows pooled observed mixed-paternity prevalence (total mixed-paternity broods divided by total broods sampled). Radial-bar height shows sampling support using log10(total broods + 1); the support key below the tree uses exactly the same transformation and reports the original brood counts. The outer categorical ring shows migratory status using the two analytical categories; missing values are grey. All species-level tracks are descriptive observations, not phylogenetically adjusted model predictions. The source tree contains 393 taxa, but the figure is restricted to the 375 species represented in the final overall-model dataset. The 18 excluded tips have neither mixed-brood counts nor brood denominators and therefore have no observed prevalence for the final meta-analysis. Pruning is applied only to the descriptive figure; the stored source tree and all analytical objects are unchanged.

title: Overall model
text: Matched-sample model without moderators This additional intercept-only model provides a matched-sample reference for the final multivariable model (Supplementary Table S12). It uses exactly the same 533 observations from 481 studies and 326 species. It is distinct from the overall model above, which uses the full dataset of 619 observations; it is not a replacement estimate of overall mixed-paternity prevalence. The response is the number of mixed-paternity broods out of the total number of broods, modelled with a beta-binomial distribution and a logit link. The matched model includes an intercept and random intercepts for study identity, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetically structured species identity, with no moderators. The data, phylogenetic covariance matrix, grouping structure and corresponding priors are retained from the final multivariable model. Priors are Student-t(3, 0, 2.5) for the intercept and group-level standard deviations (restricted to positive values for standard deviations), and Gamma(0.01, 0.01), in shape-rate notation, for beta-binomial precision. Load prepared objects Code Model Code Results The null model was fitted on Totoro with four chains, 10,000 iterations per chain including 5,000 warmup iterations (20,000 retained draws), seed 20261015, adapt_delta = 0.99 and max_treedepth = 15. Maximum R-hat was 1.003; minimum bulk and tail effective sample sizes were 844 and 1,738, respectively. There were no divergent transitions or maximum-treedepth hits. The existing final multivariable model was not refitted. The table reports posterior mean variances and equal-tailed 95% credible intervals on the logit scale. Each posterior standard-deviation draw was squared before summarising; the sum was calculated within each model draw. Descriptive reduction (%) = 100 × (1 − posterior mean variance in the multivariable model / posterior mean variance in the matched intercept-only model). Negative reductions indicate an increase. Component Matched intercept-only model Multivariable model Reduction (%) Phylogenetic species 3.941 [2.206, 6.251] 3.230 [1.544, 5.530] 18.0 Non-phylogenetic species 0.426 [0.139, 0.770] 0.461 [0.143, 0.828] -8.2 Study identity 0.076 [0.00030, 0.220] 0.102 [0.00141, 0.244] -33.9 Sum of group-level variances 4.443 [2.838, 6.606] 3.792 [2.261, 5.901] 14.6 Posterior mean phylogenetic variance was 18.0% lower in the multivariable model; the sum of the three group-level variances was 14.6% lower. These are descriptive reductions in group-level variance, not proportions of total response variance explained or predictive R-squared. Binomial sampling variation and beta-binomial dispersion remain in the observation model and are not included as additive components in this sum. No uncertainty interval is reported for the between-model reduction.

section: 8.10 Fixed-effect design diagnostics (Tables S5 and S8)
text: These diagnostics use the same 533 complete observations as the accepted primary multivariable model. The published data file is also used for the matched-sample intercept-only model; it retains all predictors needed here. No models are fitted or updated by the code below. Table S5 reports Pearson correlations for the four continuous predictors in that model. Body mass was log10-transformed before standardisation. All correlations use the same 533 records, with no pairwise deletion. Centring and division by a positive standard deviation do not change these correlations. Table S8 describes the unweighted fixed-effect design, including the intercept, treatment-coded categories and continuous predictors with their existing common scaling. No additional rescaling is applied. The exact 2-norm condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value. The matrix has 533 rows, 16 columns and rank 16, with a condition number of 15.70; there is no exact linear dependence among its columns.
